title: Cloud Cost Management Tools in 2026: A Buyer's Guide to Pricing Models and Who Does the Work
summary: Compare 2026 cloud cost management tools by pricing model and who executes savings: Pump, DoiT, CloudZero, Vantage, Finout, nOps, ProsperOps, and more.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


This guide ranks no products. It sorts tools by how vendors charge and who executes savings. The profiles explain where you do the work and where a vendor takes it on.


-


**Pump** offers a[$0 plan funded by provider partnerships](https://www.pump.co/pricing) . It suits buyers seeking managed commitment savings without a software fee.


-


**DoiT** says its pricing scales with managed cloud spend. It suits buyers seeking hands-on engineering support.


-


**CloudZero** does not publish pricing; a competitor's guide estimates a percentage of managed spend. It suits buyers focused on unit economics.


-


**Vantage** uses fixed tiers tied to tracked spend. It suits buyers wanting broad cost visibility.


-


**Finout** uses an annual subscription. It suits buyers consolidating cost sources.


-


**nOps** charges a savings share for rate optimization. It suits buyers seeking automated execution.


-


**CloudKeeper** works as an AWS and Google Cloud partner offering guaranteed discounts, with no published rate card. It suits buyers seeking a managed cloud partner.


-


**ProsperOps** charges a share of savings. It suits buyers focused on commitments.


-


**CAST AI** uses custom pricing. It suits buyers automating Kubernetes costs.


-


**OpenCost** is free. It suits buyers who can manage Kubernetes cost allocation themselves.


-


**Kubecost** offers a commercial layer. It suits buyers needing supported Kubernetes allocation.


-


**AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, and Google Cloud billing reports** are free. Each suits buyers starting with one cloud.


## The problem with most cloud cost tool comparisons


A cloud cost dashboard can show where your bill grew without telling you who will reduce it. Feature checklists often put a recommendation beside an automated purchase as if both require the same work from you. They also leave out how the vendor gets paid, which affects what your bill will look like as usage changes.


This guide asks two questions of every tool. How does the vendor get paid, and who captures the saving? A fee tied to managed spend can rise even if the tool finds no savings. A savings-share fee requires you to check how the vendor calculates the baseline. If a tool recommends a commitment but you buy and hold it, you retain the risk if usage falls. A managed commitment may put some of that risk elsewhere, subject to the contract.


Those distinctions become harder to track when you buy across cloud providers and add AI services with separate bills. Public category descriptions from Gartner or the FinOps Foundation cannot establish an individual vendor’s price or contractual responsibilities. So this guide skips secondhand scores and focuses on terms you can verify with each vendor.


## What a cloud cost management tool should actually do


A useful evaluation starts with what each tool can show and what it can change. **Visibility** means you can see costs across the cloud accounts and services you use. **Allocation** means you can assign those costs to a product, customer, or owner, even when tags are incomplete. Check whether the tool covers AI model and API charges if those costs sit outside your cloud bill.


**Optimization and execution** need separate checks. A tool may identify an idle resource but leave you to shut it down. Another may make the change after approval. For reserved capacity and savings commitments, ask who purchases the commitment and who bears the cost if usage falls. When you buy a reservation yourself, you retain that exposure. A pooled or managed arrangement may place some usage risk with the vendor, but the contract determines how much.


**Governance** determines whether you can act on cost information consistently. Compare budget alerts, approval controls, and reports that let finance reconcile savings against invoices. Gartner identifies financial risk, forecasting, efficiency, and accountability as four cloud financial management capabilities. Use those areas as questions for vendors, not as invented scores for the tools in this guide.


Finally, compare the pricing model with the work included. A percentage of managed spend can rise even if the vendor performs no additional work, while a percentage of savings requires an agreed way to calculate savings. A fixed tier or free plan may have limits on coverage, support, or execution. Ask each vendor what you must do yourself and what your bill would look like if cloud spend doubled.

## Pump


**Best for** You want cloud and AI spend visibility and help managing commitments without paying a software fee or changing application code.


**What it is** Pump combines spend visibility, commitment management, and AI/LLM routing. Its pooled-commitment model lets Pump combine customer demand and hold the risk if an individual customer’s usage drops, rather than leaving that customer responsible for a self-purchased commitment.


**Pros** Pump carries out commitment savings rather than leaving you to act on a recommendation, and it covers AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. Its model routing sends each LLM request to the lowest-cost model that meets a quality bar you set, with fallbacks if a provider is down, so AI spend sits alongside cloud spend. Budgets span both bills, anomaly detection checks spend hourly and traces spikes to a resource and owner, and untagged spend gets suggested owners, according to[Pump](https://www.pump.co/) . Setup uses read-only access and takes minutes, with no migration. Pump funds its free plan through provider partnerships and pooled group buying, according to its[pricing page](https://www.pump.co/pricing) .


**Cons** Pump is a software platform, not a consulting firm, so teams that want engineers embedded in their workflow may prefer a services-led partner. It also puts less emphasis on detailed cost-per-customer modeling than a unit-economics specialist. As with any pooled or managed commitment model, it's worth a quick conversation about how commitments are held and what happens if you leave.


**Pricing** Pump costs $0, with no platform fee and no percentage of spend or savings.


## DoiT


**Best for** You want cloud cost software backed by engineers who can help put recommendations into practice, along with access to discounts through DoiT’s reseller arrangements.


**What it is** DoiT combines cost visibility, commitment management, and engineering services. PerfectScale addresses Kubernetes costs, while Attribute covers AI and agent spending. DoiT reports a Visionary placement in a 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant.


**Pros** DoiT’s breadth lets you discuss cloud commitments, Kubernetes workloads, and AI spending with one provider. Its engineers can help investigate costs and carry out changes that a dashboard alone would leave to you.


**Cons** Service involvement and reseller billing can require more upfront configuration than a self-serve tool. Before signing, confirm which recommendations DoiT executes, which require your approval or engineering work, and who bears the risk if committed usage falls.


**Pricing** In[its own buyer's guide](https://www.doit.com/blog/cloud-cost-management-tools-buyers-guide) , DoiT says pricing scales with managed cloud spend. Ask DoiT for a quote that separates software, services, and any discounts tied to billing through DoiT, so you can compare the total cost with your current cloud bill.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs DoiT](https://www.pump.co/vs/doit) .


## CloudZero


**Best for** You need to show what each customer, feature, or team costs, especially when shared cloud resources make the bill hard to assign.


**What it is** CloudZero is a cloud cost management platform focused on unit economics. It lets you allocate costs without requiring perfect resource tags, so you can examine spending against business measures rather than only cloud accounts. It also supports AI spend allocation.


**Pros** CloudZero's allocation depth helps you investigate questions such as whether serving a particular customer costs more than that customer pays. You can use those findings to inform pricing and product decisions.


**Cons** CloudZero puts more emphasis on explaining and allocating costs than on carrying out remediation. If you need a vendor to implement savings recommendations or manage commitments for you, confirm exactly what work CloudZero will perform and what remains with your team.


**Pricing** CloudZero does not publish standard pricing.[DoiT's buyer's guide](https://www.doit.com/blog/cloud-cost-management-tools-buyers-guide) estimates a cost of roughly 1% at about $1 million in annual spend, but that competitor estimate is not a CloudZero quote. Ask CloudZero for a proposal based on your spend and required coverage.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs CloudZero](https://www.pump.co/vs/cloudzero) .


## Vantage


**Best for** Vantage suits you if you want to bring cloud costs into one view quickly and prefer published subscription tiers to a percentage-of-spend fee.


**What it is** Vantage is cloud cost management software with broad integrations for tracking and analyzing spend across services.


**Pros** Its fixed tiers make the starting price easier to project. On Pro and higher plans, Autopilot manages AWS Savings Plans, so you do not have to execute that part of commitment management yourself.


**Cons** Vantage’s visibility covers more ground than its automated remediation. The Automated FinOps Agent is available only on Enterprise, and buyers should confirm which actions it can take without their approval. Autopilot’s stated scope is AWS Savings Plans, not every cost recommendation Vantage surfaces.


**Pricing** According to[Vantage's pricing page](https://www.vantage.sh/pricing) , Starter is free for up to $2,500 per month in tracked spend. Pro starts at $30 per month, Business at $200 per month, and Enterprise requires a custom quote. Pricing follows subscription tiers tied to tracked spend rather than a percentage of your cloud bill.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs Vantage](https://www.pump.co/vs/vantage) .


## Finout


**Best for** Enterprises that need to allocate cloud, AI, and SaaS costs across business units.


**What it is** Finout consolidates costs from multiple sources into a single MegaBill view. Its virtual tagging lets you organize spending by business category without relying solely on tags in each source system.


**Pros** MegaBill gives you one place to examine costs across providers, while virtual tagging helps you assign shared or poorly tagged costs.


**Cons** Finout does not publish a rate card, so you need a quote to compare its cost with other tools. Ask which savings actions Finout executes and which your staff must carry out.


**Pricing** Finout uses a[flat annual subscription](https://www.finout.io/pricing) based on a committed spend tier. Pricing is quote-based.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs Finout](https://www.pump.co/vs/finout) .


## nOps


**Best for** Buyers who want multicloud cost visibility and help executing savings opportunities.


**What it is** nOps combines cost visibility and allocation with an Autonomous Rate Optimization offering that manages rate-related savings.


**Pros** The combination lets you review spending and use a service that acts on rate opportunities, rather than relying on recommendations alone. You can evaluate the execution service separately from the visibility and allocation features.


**Cons** nOps does not publish the percentage it takes from realized savings in the information available for this guide. Ask how nOps calculates savings, what baseline it uses, and which changes your team must carry out.


**Pricing** According to[nOps](https://www.nops.io/pricing/) , visibility and allocation carry a fixed fee based on spend. Autonomous Rate Optimization takes an undisclosed share of realized savings. Request the percentage and a worked invoice example before signing.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs nOps](https://www.pump.co/vs/nops) .


## CloudKeeper


**Best for** Buyers who want an AWS or GCP partner to help manage cloud spending through a discount agreement, rather than a standalone software subscription.


**What it is** CloudKeeper describes itself as a[cloud cost optimization partner](https://www.cloudkeeper.com/) for AWS and Google Cloud, offering what it calls guaranteed discounts with no lock-ins, AWS PPA support, a FinOps platform suite, and 24x7 support. You work with CloudKeeper on cloud costs and an agreed discount, rather than using only a self-serve cost dashboard.


**Pros** The partner model gives you a negotiated discount and a service relationship for managing spend. You can ask CloudKeeper to explain which costs qualify and what work it will perform on your behalf.


**Cons** CloudKeeper does not publish a rate card, so you need a proposal to compare its economics with other tools. Before signing, confirm which accounts and services the discount covers, who controls any cloud commitments, and what happens if you leave.


**Pricing** CloudKeeper does not publish a software fee; its economics run through partner discount agreements. Ask for the effective discount on your actual usage and the terms that could change it.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs CloudKeeper](https://www.pump.co/vs/cloudkeeper) .


## ProsperOps


**Best for** You have substantial cloud commitment spend and want a specialist to manage it.


**What it is** ProsperOps focuses on managing cloud commitments and offers a separate Resource Management product. Its commitment service addresses purchase and adjustment decisions rather than serving as a full cost visibility and allocation platform.


**Pros** ProsperOps takes on the work of managing commitments, which can reduce the manual decisions you make as usage changes. Its Savings Share model ties its fee to realized savings.


**Cons** Pair ProsperOps with a broader visibility platform if you need to allocate costs by customer, product, or team. Before signing, ask how ProsperOps calculates savings and who bears the risk if your usage falls below committed levels.


**Pricing** According to[ProsperOps](https://www.prosperops.com/pricing/) , Savings Share charges a percentage of realized savings, tiered with a term commitment. Resource Management charges a flat monthly fee per managed resource. Ask for the applicable tier and term when comparing quotes.


For a feature-by-feature view, see[Pump vs ProsperOps](https://www.pump.co/vs/prosperops) .


## CAST AI and Kubecost/OpenCost


**CAST AI**


-


**Best for** You if Kubernetes node costs need active optimization rather than reporting alone.


-


**What it is** CAST AI manages cluster capacity through node autoscaling, workload placement, and spot-instance use.


-


**Pros** Its automation can make capacity changes that a cost dashboard would leave for you to implement.


-


**Cons** You need to review which workloads can tolerate automated placement and spot interruptions. CAST AI does not provide a full view of spending outside Kubernetes.


-


**Pricing**[CAST AI](https://cast.ai/pricing/) uses custom quotes. Ask which automation features and clusters the quote covers. See also[Pump vs Cast AI](https://www.pump.co/vs/cast-ai) .


**Kubecost/OpenCost**


-


**Best for** You if you need to assign Kubernetes costs to workloads and understand where cluster spending goes.


-


**What each is**[OpenCost](https://www.opencost.io/) is a free, CNCF open-source project for Kubernetes cost allocation. IBM-owned Kubecost adds a commercial layer for organizations that need more than the open-source project provides.


-


**Pros** Workload-level allocation helps you identify which applications consume shared cluster resources.


-


**Cons** Cost reports do not make the capacity changes that CAST AI automates. Neither OpenCost nor Kubecost replaces a broader view of cloud and AI spending.


-


**Pricing** OpenCost is free. Confirm Kubecost’s commercial pricing and included features with the vendor. See also[Pump vs Kubecost](https://www.pump.co/vs/kubecost) .


Both options address Kubernetes costs specifically. Pair either with a broader cloud cost platform if you also need to track spending outside your clusters.


## Native cloud provider tools


**Best for** You use one cloud provider and need a free starting point for tracking costs.


**What they are** AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, and Google Cloud billing reports show charges and usage within their respective clouds. You can filter costs by service and billing account, subscription, or project to investigate changes over time.


**Pros** Each tool uses its provider’s billing data, so you can inspect charges without connecting separate cloud cost management software.


**Cons** Each tool covers only its own cloud. You must combine data elsewhere to compare providers, and reports or recommendations do not execute savings for you. You still need to review commitment purchases and make configuration changes. See[Pump vs AWS Cost Explorer](https://www.pump.co/vs/aws-cost-explorer) for the AWS case.


**Pricing** Core reporting is free. Related services, such as storage for exported billing data, may incur charges.

## What to check before you sign


-


**Check who holds each commitment.** Ask whether you or the vendor signs for reserved capacity, who pays if usage falls, and whether you can transfer or cancel commitments when you leave. Get the exit terms in writing before you authorize purchases.


-


**Define the savings calculation.** For a percentage-of-savings contract, ask the vendor to document the baseline, eligible discounts, fees, and treatment of workload changes. Require an annual reconciliation against provider invoices and a way to dispute the calculation.


-


**Model the fee as your bill grows.** For a percentage-of-spend model, ask which charges count as managed spend and whether the rate changes at higher volumes. Calculate the fee at today’s spend and at twice that amount.


-


**Examine the funding behind free plans.** For Pump’s[$0 plan](https://www.pump.co/pricing) , ask how provider partnerships and pooled buying fund the service and how that applies to your providers.


-


**Name the person who executes each saving.** Ask which changes the vendor makes automatically, which require your approval, and which recommendations your staff must implement. Confirm who can reverse an automated change.


-


**Protect your reporting history.** Ask whether you can export raw cost data, allocation rules, and historical reports in a usable format. Confirm how long you retain access after cancellation and whether the contract charges for an export.


## How to run a fair evaluation


Run a trial through one full billing cycle using accounts that contain real workloads, shared costs, and, if relevant, AI model charges. Before connecting a tool, save the previous invoice and record usage levels. Give every vendor the same account access and compare its visibility against the provider’s billing records. Check whether it shows charges at the level you need, rather than relying on a polished dashboard.


Test allocation and AI spend with specific questions. Ask each tool to assign a shared database bill to the services that use it and to identify which product or workload generated AI charges. Record charges the tool cannot assign, and check whether its reports preserve your allocation rules.


For optimization, pick one recommendation and track who must approve and apply it. If the vendor manages commitments, ask who holds them when usage falls or you leave. Test governance by setting a budget alert and checking who receives it and what action, if any, follows.


After the next invoice arrives, compare claimed savings with actual charges. Account for changes in usage, rates, and credits before attributing a lower bill to the tool. Document any work your staff performed so the comparison includes the effort required to capture savings.


## Where Pump fits


Pump fits a shortlist when you want cloud spend visibility, pooled commitment savings, and AI routing without a percentage-based software fee. Its $0 plan is[funded through provider partnerships and pooled group buying](https://www.pump.co/pricing) . Under the pooled model, Pump holds the commitments and bears the risk if usage drops. You should still confirm how Pump holds those commitments and what happens when you leave.


Pump is a less direct fit if you need forward-deployed consulting or detailed cost-per-customer reporting. DoiT focuses on hands-on support, while CloudZero focuses on unit economics. Because its free model is funded by provider partnerships and pooled buying, it's reasonable to ask how that works for your providers and how commitments are handled at exit.


## FAQ


**How do FinOps tools differ from cloud cost management tools?** FinOps is the practice of managing cloud spending across engineering and finance. Cloud cost management tools provide the billing data, allocation, and controls that support that work. Vendors use both labels, so compare what each product does rather than its category name.


**How can you audit percentage-of-savings pricing?** Agree on a baseline and calculation method before signing. Check the vendor’s claimed savings against invoices and commitment charges, and ask how the calculation handles usage changes, existing discounts, and overlapping recommendations.


**Do free tools have hidden costs?** A free software fee does not tell you who pays for the service or who does the work. Native provider tools may leave implementation to you. For a provider-funded option such as[Pump](https://pump.co/) , ask how provider partnerships fund the service and how that applies to your providers.


**How should a platform account for AI and LLM spend?** Check whether it imports the AI services you buy and assigns their charges to the right project or customer. Cloud-hosted model workloads may appear in ordinary cloud bills, while separate model-provider invoices may need another integration.


**How do you assess commitment lock-in risk?** Ask who owns each commitment, who pays if usage falls, and what happens when you leave. Get the remaining term, transfer options, and exit obligations in writing.


**Who captures the savings after a tool finds them?** Ask the vendor to demonstrate one recommendation through to the invoice. A dashboard may leave the purchase or configuration change to you, while an automated or managed service may execute it under agreed permissions.


## Conclusion


A cloud cost management tool’s total cost depends on how its fees change as your bill grows and how much work you must do to capture savings. A tool may identify a savings opportunity, but you still need to know who acts on it and who bears the risk if usage drops.


Build your shortlist around those two questions before comparing feature lists. Use the signing checklist to examine fees, commitment terms, and exit conditions. Then test each candidate against your workloads and invoices to see which savings it actually delivers.
